To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) population estimates based on statistical modelling of point-count data are not reliable and (2) the lack of a reliable population estimate is not a good reason to not monitor population trends.

(i) population size is a fundamental parameter for conservation, but (ii) population size is often estimated with methods that do not account for the uncertainty of the data, (iii) the use of models to estimate population size is widespread, but the models are rarely validated against independent data, and (iv) population size estimates based on models are often used in conservation, even though they are not validated.

“Ecologists and conservation biologist are increasingly attracted to sophisticated models, at the expense of data quality and fieldwork design, which may lead to conclusions that are not realistic and may be used in management applications”.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how to best use models in ecological research, and we argue that models should be used to make inferences about processes that can be tested by empirical observations.
the quality of data used in ecological research and conservation, particularly the use of models to predict population trends and sizes.
how we can improve the quality of our research in order to better inform conservation decisions.

, “We do not know what the population size is, but we can predict it with a high degree of confidence, and we are sure that it has declined over time.”
“we have no idea of how many birds are breeding in Europe, but we are confident that the number is between 1 and 1.5 billion”.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we should be careful not to overestimate the value of our data, and to be cautious in our interpretation of results.
the more we know about the biology of our species of interest, the better our models will be.
we need to be careful when using models that we have not validated them.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the quality of fieldwork and data collection is of paramount importance in ecological research.
we must not allow the pursuit of the latest analytical techniques to lead to a loss in perspective and the uncritical acceptance of biological unrealities.

the best way to avoid such pitfalls is to invest in well-rounded scientists and more collaborative, multi- disciplinary teams capable of integrating the best analytical tools with in-depth knowledge on the natural history of the study species.
